2 Introduction

A great deal of what health researchers measure is continuous. Blood pressure, body mass index, glycated haemoglobin, lung function, birth weight, serum cholesterol, quality-of-life scores, length of hospital stay — these are the quantities on which clinical decisions are made, populations are compared and interventions are judged. Linear regression is the standard method for analysing them, and it is the foundation on which almost every other regression model in health research is built.

2.1 Why linear regression matters in health research

The appeal of linear regression begins with a limitation of simpler methods. A \(t\)-test can compare mean blood pressure between two groups, and a correlation coefficient can quantify the association between body mass index and blood pressure. Neither can answer the question that actually arises in practice: how much does blood pressure differ per unit of body mass index, among people who are otherwise similar in age, sex and physical activity? Linear regression answers precisely that. It expresses an association as an interpretable quantity in the units of the outcome, attaches a confidence interval to it, and adjusts it for other measured variables simultaneously.

That capacity for adjustment is what makes regression indispensable in epidemiology. Observational health data are confounded almost by definition: people who differ in one exposure differ in many others. A crude comparison of fasting blood sugar between urban and rural residents confuses residence with the age structure, diet, obesity and socioeconomic position of the two populations. Multiple linear regression estimates the difference associated with residence among participants alike in the measured covariates, which is the closest an observational analysis can come to the comparison a randomised trial would deliver. Section 5.4 of this chapter shows how consequential this can be, with an association that is highly significant before adjustment and entirely absent after it.

Linear regression matters for a second reason that has nothing to do with linear regression specifically. Logistic regression for binary outcomes, Poisson regression for counts, Cox regression for survival times and mixed-effects models for grouped data are all extensions of the same framework. The concepts developed here — the regression equation, the partial coefficient, adjustment, indicator variables, interaction, model diagnostics — transfer directly. A reader who understands linear regression thoroughly has already learned most of what the others require.

The final reason is professional rather than technical. Regression results dominate the medical literature, and they are frequently misreported. A survey of a full year of papers in the BMJ, The Lancet and the New England Journal of Medicine identified fifteen distinct categories of error in the use of correlation and regression, among them the omission of confidence intervals, over-reliance on \(p\)-values, and unclear reporting of sample size (Porter, 1999). Critically appraising such analyses is a core competency for a doctoral graduate in public health, and it requires knowing not only how the models are fitted but how they fail.

2.2 Four use-cases in medicine, health and public health

2.2.1 1. Quantifying a dose–response relationship

The most direct use of linear regression is to express how much a continuous outcome changes per unit of a continuous exposure. Doll and colleagues (2002) modelled systolic and diastolic blood pressure against body mass index, waist circumference and waist-to-hip ratio in 3,116 adults in the Seychelles and Switzerland, adjusting for age. Because the regression coefficient is a rate of change, their findings could be stated in directly usable terms: in men, an increase of 1.7 kg/m² in body mass index, or of 4.5 cm in waist circumference, corresponded to a rise of 1 mmHg in systolic blood pressure; in women the corresponding figures were 1.25 kg/m² and 2.5 cm.

This is regression doing what no dichotomised analysis can. Splitting body mass index into “obese” and “not obese” would discard the gradient entirely and reduce statistical power, a cost quantified by Altman and Royston (2006). The graded, continuous nature of the adiposity–blood pressure relationship was established in exactly this way by the Framingham investigators decades earlier (Kannel et al., 1967).

2.2.2 2. Adjusting for confounding in observational studies

The second use-case is adjustment, and its effects are often dramatic. Law and colleagues (2001) examined the relationship between size at birth and childhood blood pressure in 1,570 children aged three to six years across five countries. Blood pressure was positively related to the child’s current weight, and it was only after regression adjustment for current weight and sex that the inverse association between birth weight and systolic pressure became clear: in Chile, adjusted systolic pressure rose by 4.9 mmHg (95% CI 2.1 to 7.7) for each kilogram decrease in birth weight.

Here adjustment did not merely refine an estimate — it revealed an association that the unadjusted analysis obscured. It also illustrates why adjustment demands subject-matter judgement rather than statistical routine, since whether current weight is a confounder or a variable on the causal pathway determines whether adjusting for it is appropriate at all. That distinction recurs throughout Section 5.

2.2.3 3. Deriving reference values and prediction equations

Much of clinical medicine depends on knowing what is normal for a given patient, and reference standards are built by regression. The Global Lung Function Initiative derived spirometry reference equations from nearly 100,000 records on healthy non-smokers across 33 countries, modelling forced expiratory volume and forced vital capacity as continuous functions of age, height, sex and ethnicity (Quanjer et al., 2012). The resulting equations, and the lower limits of normal derived from them, are now the international standard for interpreting a spirometry result.

The same approach underlies the estimation of kidney function. The CKD-EPI equation was developed by regressing log-transformed measured glomerular filtration rate on serum creatinine, age, sex and race in 8,254 participants, then validating it in an independent sample of 3,896 (Levey et al., 2009). Every laboratory report of an estimated GFR is the output of a fitted regression equation. Note in both examples the use of a logarithmic transformation of the outcome, the technique developed in Section 7.

2.2.4 4. Evaluating interventions on a continuous endpoint

The fourth use-case is the analysis of trials and programme evaluations whose endpoint is continuous. The DASH trial randomised 459 adults to a control diet, a fruit-and-vegetable diet, or a combination diet, holding sodium intake and body weight constant (Appel et al., 1997). The combination diet lowered systolic blood pressure by 5.5 mmHg and diastolic by 3.0 mmHg more than the control diet, with substantially larger effects of 11.4 and 5.5 mmHg among participants with hypertension.

Randomisation removes confounding, so why use regression at all? Because adjusting the follow-up measurement for its own baseline value increases precision considerably, and because analysis of covariance — regression of the follow-up outcome on the baseline value plus the treatment indicator — is statistically preferable to comparing change scores or follow-up values alone (Vickers & Altman, 2001). The subgroup difference in the DASH results is also an instance of the phenomenon formalised in Section 8: the effect of the intervention depended on baseline hypertension status.

2.3 What this chapter covers

The chapter develops the method in the order in which it is used. Section 3 introduces simple linear regression, least squares estimation, and the coefficient of determination with its many pitfalls. Section 4 shows how to check whether a fitted model is trustworthy. Section 5 extends the model to several predictors, which brings adjustment, indicator variables and the general linear F-test. Section 6 applies the diagnostic machinery to the multivariable case and adds formal tests for normality and constant variance. Section 7 addresses what to do when the assumptions fail. Section 8 relaxes the assumption that a covariate’s effect is the same for everyone.

Throughout, the same dataset is used and the same outcome is modelled, so that each technique is seen to build on the last. The analyses are real: where the data behave awkwardly, the awkwardness is reported rather than smoothed over, because recognising and handling such situations is the skill this chapter exists to teach.

3 Simple Linear Regression

Regression analysis begins with the simplest useful case: one continuous outcome and one predictor. Almost everything that follows in this chapter — adjustment for confounding, diagnostic checking, transformation, interaction — is an extension of machinery that is easiest to see, and easiest to get wrong, in this two-variable setting. This section develops that machinery and applies it to a real survey dataset.

3.1 The working dataset

Every worked example in this chapter uses data from the Metabolic Syndrome Study for Malaysia (MSSM), a community-based survey of adults. Each record is one adult participant. The survey collected sociodemographic information, anthropometric measurements, resting blood pressure, a panel of fasting venous blood investigations, and self-reported medical history. The dataset contains 4295 records.

The outcome variable throughout is fasting blood sugar (FBS), measured in mmol/L. FBS is a natural teaching outcome for linear regression: it is continuous, it is clinically meaningful at the individual level, and it is the measurement on which the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus partly rests.

3.1.1 Two derived covariates

Two of the covariates used in this chapter are not measured directly but derived from measurements that are. Both are standard indices of adiposity in metabolic research, and each captures a different aspect of body habitus.

Body mass index (BMI) expresses weight relative to height and is a measure of overall adiposity:

\[ \text{BMI} = \frac{\text{weight in kilograms}}{(\text{height in metres})^2} \qquad \text{units: kg/m}^2 \]

Waist–hip ratio (WHR) compares abdominal with gluteofemoral girth and is a measure of central fat distribution:

\[ \text{WHR} = \frac{\text{waist circumference in cm}}{\text{hip circumference in cm}} \qquad \text{(unitless)} \]

The distinction matters clinically. Two people with identical BMI may differ substantially in where that mass is carried, and central adiposity is the more strongly implicated in insulin resistance. Because the two indices measure different things, they are only weakly correlated with each other in these data (\(r\) = 0.24), which means both can be entered into a model without difficulty. Both are, however, strongly related to waist circumference itself (\(r\) = 0.80 for BMI and 0.67 for WHR), a fact that becomes important in Section 5.6.

Deriving a variable does not exempt it from scrutiny. BMI here ranges from 13.2 to 56.9 kg/m², and WHR from 0.59 to 1.58. The single WHR value above 1.5 is physiologically extreme and most likely reflects a measurement or recording error; it is reported here rather than silently removed, and its influence is assessed in Section 6.2 along with all other observations.

Table 1 describes the outcome and the 18 candidate covariates used in this chapter.

Two features of Table 1 deserve attention before any model is fitted, because both shape the analysis later.

First, the outcome is markedly skewed to the right. The mean FBS of 5.63 mmol/L exceeds the median of 5.16 mmol/L, and values extend to 28.01 mmol/L, giving a skewness coefficient of 2.80. This is not a data error. It is the expected shape for a glycaemic measurement in a general adult population: most participants cluster in a narrow normoglycaemic range, while a minority with impaired glucose regulation or established diabetes generate a long upper tail. This skew will have visible consequences in Section 4 and Section 6.

Second, the data are almost complete. The outcome is recorded for every one of the 4295 participants, as are age, sex, ethnicity, residence, all anthropometric measurements, blood pressure and fasting triglyceride. Only a few variables have any missing values at all, the largest among those used here being total bilirubin. All analyses use complete-case analysis, the default behaviour of the lm() function in R: any record missing the outcome or any covariate in a given model is excluded from that model. The sample size is therefore reported for every model fitted. With so little missingness the choice of missing-data method is inconsequential here, but that is a property of this dataset rather than a general licence — complete-case analysis is unbiased only when data are missing completely at random, and in datasets with substantial missingness that assumption deserves explicit examination.

3.2 What simple linear regression is

Simple linear regression summarises the relationship between two continuous variables. One variable is treated as the outcome, and the other as the predictor.

NoteDefinition: simple linear regression

Simple linear regression is a statistical method for summarising and studying the relationship between two continuous variables, in which one variable, denoted \(x\), is regarded as the predictor, explanatory or independent variable, and the other, denoted \(y\), is regarded as the response, outcome or dependent variable.

The method is called simple because it involves exactly one predictor. When two or more predictors are used, the method becomes multiple linear regression, the subject of Section 5. Two points of vocabulary matter for the rest of the chapter.

The word linear refers to linearity in the parameters, not to a requirement that a scatter plot look like a straight line. A model containing \(x^2\) or \(\log x\) as a predictor is still a linear model, because the unknown parameters enter additively and are multiplied by known quantities. This is why the transformations in Section 7 remain within the linear regression framework rather than departing from it.

The word regression signals that the object being estimated is a conditional mean. Simple linear regression does not claim that FBS is a deterministic function of body mass index. It claims something weaker and far more useful: that the average FBS among people who share a given body mass index changes in a systematic way as that body mass index changes. Individual variation about that average is expected and is modelled explicitly.

The predictor need not be continuous. A binary predictor such as rural versus urban residence is entirely admissible, and Section 3.7 works through such an example. What the outcome may be is more restricted: ordinary linear regression assumes a continuous outcome whose conditional distribution is approximately normal with constant variance. Binary and count outcomes require the related models named at the end of this chapter.

3.3 The best fitting line

Suppose FBS is plotted against body mass index for every participant. Many straight lines could be drawn through the resulting cloud of points. The task is to choose one, which requires a definition of what makes a line good.

For a candidate line, the prediction error for participant \(i\) is the vertical distance between the observed outcome and the value the line predicts:

\[ e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i \]

where \(y_i\) is the observed outcome and \(\hat{y}_i\) is the predicted, or fitted, value. A natural objective is to make these errors collectively small. Simply summing them fails, because positive and negative errors cancel: a line lying far from every point can achieve a sum of zero. Two repairs are available — summing absolute errors, or summing squared errors.

The method of least squares takes the second option. It selects the values of the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of the squared prediction errors:

\[ Q = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - (b_0 + b_1 x_i) \right)^2 \]

NoteDefinition: the least squares line

The least squares line is the line \(\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x\) for which the sum of the squared vertical distances between the observed outcomes and the fitted values is smaller than for any other line.

Squaring rather than taking absolute values is partly a matter of mathematical convenience — the squared criterion is differentiable, and minimising it yields closed-form estimators:

\[ b_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2}, \qquad b_0 = \bar{y} - b_1 \bar{x} \]

The second expression carries a useful geometric fact: the least squares line always passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). It also has a statistical consequence worth remembering — because errors are squared, observations far from the bulk of the data influence the fitted line disproportionately. A single extreme observation can move the line appreciably, which is why the diagnostic work of Section 4 is not optional.

Least squares is not the only estimation method. Maximum likelihood estimation is the alternative, and under the normal-error model described next the two coincide for the regression coefficients. Both yield estimators that are unbiased and, among linear unbiased estimators, have minimum variance.

3.4 The simple linear regression model

The least squares line is a description of the sample. To generalise from the sample to the population — to construct confidence intervals and test hypotheses — a probability model is required.

NoteThe simple linear regression model

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \ \text{independently} \]

where, for the \(i\)-th observation:

  • \(y_i\) is the observed outcome;
  • \(x_i\) is the observed value of the predictor, treated as fixed and known;
  • \(\beta_0\) is the population intercept: the mean outcome when \(x = 0\);
  • \(\beta_1\) is the population slope: the change in the mean outcome per one-unit increase in \(x\);
  • \(\epsilon_i\) is the error term, unobservable, with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\).

Taking expectations of both sides, and noting that \(E\{\epsilon_i\} = 0\), gives the regression function — the equation for the conditional mean:

\[ E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i \]

This equation is the object of inference. The line it describes is the population regression line, which connects the mean outcome of each subpopulation defined by a value of \(x\). The sample estimates \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) estimate \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\); a different sample would give somewhat different estimates, and none would reproduce the population line exactly.

The model asserts four conditions simultaneously. They are conveniently remembered by the mnemonic LINE, and each is checked in Section 4.

NoteThe LINE conditions
Condition Statement
L Linear The mean outcome is a linear function of \(x\)
I Independent The errors are independent of one another
N Normal The errors are normally distributed at each value of \(x\)
E Equal variance The errors have the same variance \(\sigma^2\) at every value of \(x\)

Equivalently: the errors \(\epsilon_i\) are independent normal random variables with mean zero and constant variance \(\sigma^2\).

These conditions are not equally consequential. Tests and intervals are very sensitive to departures from independence, and moderately sensitive to unequal variances. Inference about \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) is comparatively robust to non-normality, particularly in large samples. Prediction intervals, by contrast, are quite sensitive to non-normality. This ordering matters when deciding which diagnostic failures demand action, and it is applied explicitly in Section 6.

A notational convention is used throughout this chapter and is worth stating once. Greek letters (\(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), \(\sigma^2\)) denote unknown population parameters. Roman letters and hatted symbols (\(b_0\), \(b_1\), \(\hat{\sigma}\)) denote estimates computed from a sample. The fitted regression equation, which is what statistical software reports, is therefore

\[ \hat{y}_i = b_0 + b_1 x_i \]

The error variance is estimated by the mean squared error, \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \sum e_i^2 / (n - 2)\), whose square root — the residual standard error — expresses the typical size of a prediction error in the units of the outcome. The divisor is \(n - 2\) because two parameters have been estimated from the data.

3.5 The coefficient of determination, \(R^2\)

A fitted line has a slope, and the slope has a \(p\)-value. Neither answers a question clinicians and reviewers ask immediately: how much of the variation in the outcome does the predictor actually explain? The coefficient of determination answers exactly that, and it is built by partitioning variability.

Consider two ways of predicting a participant’s FBS. Knowing nothing about the participant, the best available prediction is the overall mean \(\bar{y}\). Knowing the participant’s body mass index, the prediction becomes \(\hat{y}_i\) from the fitted line. The total deviation of an observation from the overall mean decomposes exactly into the part the line explains and the part it does not:

\[ \underbrace{(y_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{(\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})}_{\text{explained by the line}} + \underbrace{(y_i - \hat{y}_i)}_{\text{left unexplained}} \]

Remarkably, this identity survives squaring and summing over all observations, giving the fundamental partition of the sums of squares:

\[ \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SST} = \underbrace{\sum (\hat{y}_i - \bar{y})^2}_{SSR} + \underbrace{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}_{SSE} \]

\[ SST = SSR + SSE \]

where \(SST\) is the total sum of squares, \(SSR\) the regression (explained) sum of squares, and \(SSE\) the error (unexplained) sum of squares.

NoteDefinition: the coefficient of determination

\[ R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = 1 - \frac{SSE}{SST} \]

\(R^2\) is the proportion of the total variation in the outcome that is explained by the regression on the predictor. It is bounded by \(0 \le R^2 \le 1\), and is often reported as a percentage.

3.5.1 Calculating \(R^2\) from the sums of squares

It is worth assembling \(R^2\) once by hand, so that the number reported by software is not merely accepted. For the regression of FBS on body mass index, the analysis of variance table gives

\[ SSR = 632.6, \qquad SSE = 27756.2 \]

so the total sum of squares is

\[ SST = SSR + SSE = 632.6 + 27756.2 = 28388.8 \]

and therefore

\[ R^2 = \frac{SSR}{SST} = \frac{632.6}{28388.8} = 0.0223 \]

Body mass index explains 2.2% of the variation in fasting blood sugar in these data. Equivalently, 97.8% of that variation remains unexplained.

The correlation coefficient is closely related: \(r = \pm\sqrt{R^2}\), taking the sign of the slope. Here the slope is positive, so \(r = \sqrt{0.0223} = 0.149\), which agrees with the directly computed Pearson correlation of 0.149. The two quantities carry the same information about strength of association, but they answer different questions: \(r\) measures the strength and direction of linear association, while \(R^2\) measures proportion of variation explained. Note also that \(R^2 = 0.0223\) corresponds to \(r = 0.149\) — squaring shrinks a modest correlation into a very small proportion of variance, which is why the two are so often misread against each other.

3.6 Cautions in interpreting \(R^2\)

\(R^2\) is the most quoted and the most abused number in applied regression. Seven cautions apply, and several are illustrated directly by this chapter’s own results.

WarningSeven cautions in interpreting \(R^2\)
  1. \(R^2\) and \(r\) quantify only the strength of a linear relationship. A perfect curved relationship can produce \(r = 0\) and \(R^2 = 0\%\). A small \(R^2\) is therefore evidence against a linear association, not against association in general.
  2. A large \(R^2\) does not mean the straight line fits well. Another functional form may fit considerably better. This is the most common single misuse of \(R^2\): a model can explain 90% of the variance and still show obvious curvature in its residuals. Only the diagnostics of Section 4 can distinguish the two situations.
  3. \(R^2\) and \(r\) can be substantially altered by one or a few observations. In small datasets, deleting a single point can move \(r\) from strongly positive to strongly negative. Influence of this kind must be checked, not assumed absent.
  4. Association does not imply causation. This caution turns on study design rather than on statistics. In an experiment the investigator sets the values of the predictor; in an observational study the investigator only records what occurred. Most regression analyses in health research, including every model in this chapter, use observational data, so causal language is not licensed by any value of \(R^2\).
  5. Ecological correlations overstate the strength of individual-level association. When the units of analysis are groups — districts, states, countries — and the variables are rates or averages, the resulting correlation is typically much larger than the corresponding correlation between individuals, because aggregation removes within-group variation. An analysis of aggregated data answers a question about groups, not about people.
  6. A statistically significant \(R^2\) does not mean the slope is practically meaningful. Large samples make it easy to reject the null hypothesis for a slope of negligible size. In these data body mass index explains only 2.2% of the variance in FBS, yet the slope is very far from zero in statistical terms (\(p\) = 7.9 × 10-23) because 4295 participants contribute to the estimate.
  7. A large \(R^2\) does not guarantee useful prediction. Confidence intervals for the mean outcome, and especially prediction intervals for a new individual, may remain far too wide to be clinically actionable. Here the residual standard error is 2.54 mmol/L — large relative to the range over which FBS is clinically interpreted.

Two further points belong alongside these. First, there is no universal threshold for a “large” \(R^2\): what counts as substantial depends entirely on the field. In laboratory measurement an \(R^2\) of 30% might be unacceptable, whereas in population health research, where outcomes have many determinants, it may represent a strong finding. Second, \(R^2\) never decreases when a predictor is added, even a predictor consisting of pure noise. Comparing models with different numbers of predictors therefore requires the adjusted \(R^2\), which divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom; this is taken up in Section 5.

The habit to carry into the applied work that follows is straightforward: report the effect size with its confidence interval, let \(R^2\) describe explanatory power, and never allow either to stand in for the other.

3.7 Application: fasting blood sugar and eighteen candidate covariates

The MSSM dataset provides 18 variables that are plausibly associated with fasting blood sugar, including the two derived indices of Section 3.1.1. A standard first step in a regression analysis is to examine each one separately against the outcome, fitting 18 simple linear regressions. This is sometimes called univariable or unadjusted screening, and its results are reported in Table 2.

Table 2 repays careful reading, and four lessons emerge.

15 of the 18 covariates are statistically significant, yet almost none explains much variance. Setting aside history of diabetes, no covariate explains more than 7.6% of the variation in FBS. This is caution 6 of Section 3.6 made concrete: with roughly 4300 observations per model, very small associations achieve very small \(p\)-values. A screening table of this kind identifies candidate variables; it does not rank their importance, and it certainly does not identify causes.

History of diabetes stands apart. It explains 21.0% of the variance in FBS — several times more than any other covariate. This is entirely expected and is a warning about interpretation rather than a finding: a self-reported diagnosis of diabetes is not a risk factor for high blood sugar but a consequence of previously measured high blood sugar. The variable is retained in the models that follow because it is a powerful predictor and because adjusting for it makes the remaining coefficients interpretable within diabetic and non-diabetic groups, but no causal reading of its coefficient is available.

The two derived indices behave differently from each other. Body mass index explains 2.23% of the variance and waist–hip ratio 1.38%, both smaller than waist circumference alone at 2.95%. Deriving a variable does not automatically produce a better predictor: BMI discards information about fat distribution, and WHR discards information about overall size. Each is useful for what it measures, not because it is a composite.

Two covariates show no evidence of association: residence (0.339) and sex (0.652), with height marginal. Reporting these honestly is as much a part of the analysis as reporting the significant ones.

The remainder of this section examines two of these 18 models in full — one with a numerical predictor and one with a categorical predictor. Body mass index is chosen as the numerical example: it is a derived variable whose construction was set out in Section 3.1.1, it is universally understood in health research, and it reappears in the multivariable model of Section 5. Marital status is chosen as the categorical example: it has two levels, which makes indicator coding easy to see, and it is significant with a very small effect — the clearest illustration in this dataset of the distinction between statistical and practical significance. These same two models are carried into Section 4 for diagnostic checking.

3.7.1 Worked example A: a numerical predictor

Figure 1 shows FBS against body mass index with the least squares line superimposed, and Table 3 reports the fitted model.

The fitted regression equation is

\[ \widehat{\text{FBS}} = 3.718 + 0.0738 \times \text{BMI} \]

Each element has a direct reading:

  • The slope is 0.0738 mmol/L per kg/m² (95% CI 0.0592 to 0.0884). For every additional unit of body mass index, mean fasting blood sugar is higher by 0.0738 mmol/L. Because one unit of BMI is a small difference, a more communicable statement rescales it: a BMI higher by 5 kg/m² — roughly the gap between the middle of the normal range and the middle of the overweight range — corresponds to a mean FBS higher by 0.369 mmol/L.
  • The intercept is 3.718 mmol/L, the estimated mean FBS at a body mass index of zero. This has no physical meaning. The intercept here is a mathematical anchor for the line, not a quantity to interpret, because \(x = 0\) lies far outside the observed range of 13.2 to 56.9 kg/m². Centring the predictor on its mean would make the intercept interpretable as the mean FBS at average BMI.
  • The residual standard error is 2.543 mmol/L, so individual FBS values typically deviate from the fitted line by about that much — a reminder of how weak individual-level prediction is here despite a precisely estimated slope.

Prediction follows mechanically from the equation. Substituting a body mass index of 30 kg/m², the conventional threshold for obesity:

\[ \widehat{\text{FBS}} = 3.718 + 0.0738 \times 30 = 5.932 \ \text{mmol/L} \]

This is an estimate of the mean FBS among people with a BMI of 30, not a prediction for any individual. Predicting an individual value requires a prediction interval, which is much wider than the confidence interval for the mean because it must also accommodate the residual variation of 2.54 mmol/L. Note also that prediction is only defensible within the observed range of the predictor; extrapolating beyond it assumes the linear relationship continues where no data exist.

3.7.2 Worked example B: a categorical predictor

When the predictor is categorical, the same algebra applies but the coefficients acquire a different meaning. Marital status has two levels, married and single. R codes it as an indicator (or dummy) variable taking the value 0 for the reference level, married, and 1 for single:

\[ x_i = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if participant } i \text{ is married} \\ 1 & \text{if participant } i \text{ is single} \end{cases} \]

Substituting each value into the regression function shows what the two coefficients now represent:

\[ E\{\text{FBS} \mid \text{married}\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times 0 = \beta_0 \] \[ E\{\text{FBS} \mid \text{single}\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times 1 = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \]

TipInterpreting an indicator variable

With a two-level categorical predictor, the intercept is the mean outcome in the reference group, and the slope is the difference in mean outcome between the two groups. Simple linear regression with a binary predictor is algebraically identical to a two-sample \(t\)-test assuming equal variances.

The fitted equation is \(\widehat{\text{FBS}} = 5.698 - 0.317 \times \text{single}\), and the coefficients recover the group means exactly:

  • Mean FBS in married participants is the intercept, 5.698 mmol/L, which equals the directly computed married mean of 5.698 mmol/L.
  • Mean FBS in single participants is \(5.698 - 0.317 = 5.381\) mmol/L, matching the directly computed single mean of 5.381 mmol/L.
  • The coefficient of -0.317 mmol/L is therefore the mean difference, single minus married.

The 95% confidence interval for that difference is -0.506 to -0.128 mmol/L and the \(p\)-value is 0.001. The interval excludes zero, so there is evidence that mean fasting blood sugar differs by marital status: single participants average about 0.32 mmol/L lower than married participants.

This model is worth dwelling on, because it is the cleanest example in the dataset of a result that is statistically convincing and substantively slight. The \(p\)-value of 0.001 looks impressive; the \(R^2\) of 0.25% reveals that marital status accounts for about one part in 398 of the variation in FBS. A difference of 0.32 mmol/L is also small against a within-group standard deviation of roughly 2.6 mmol/L, as Figure 2 shows: the two distributions overlap almost completely.

WarningA significant coefficient is not an important one

Marital status is significantly associated with fasting blood sugar (\(p\) = 0.0010) and explains 0.25% of its variation. Both statements are true, and only the second one is informative about magnitude.

Note also that marital status is almost certainly a proxy here rather than a cause. Married participants in this sample are likely to be older, and age is itself associated with FBS. Whether the association survives adjustment for age is a question this simple model cannot answer — which is the motivation for Section 5.

Not every covariate produces even this much. Residence and sex, as Table 2 shows, give \(p\)-values of 0.339 and 0.652 respectively — no evidence of any difference in mean FBS. Such results should be reported as they stand. They do not demonstrate that the groups are identical; they show that any difference is too small to distinguish from zero at this sample size, with the confidence interval bounding how large it could plausibly be. Nor does a non-significant unadjusted result mean a variable is irrelevant to the analysis: residence is retained in the multivariable model of Section 5, where its adjusted coefficient behaves differently from its crude one.

Both models are now fitted and interpreted. Neither has yet been checked. Coefficient tables of the kind shown above are the same whether the model’s assumptions hold or fail completely, which is why the next section examines the residuals before any of these conclusions is allowed to stand.

4 Assessment of the Simple Linear Regression Model

The two models fitted in Section 3.7 produced coefficient tables, confidence intervals and \(p\)-values. Those quantities are all computed under the LINE conditions. If the conditions fail, the arithmetic still runs and the table still prints, but the inference it supports may be wrong. Nothing in a coefficient table reveals whether this has happened.

Model assessment closes that gap. The strategy is indirect: the errors \(\epsilon_i\) are unobservable, so their observable counterparts, the residuals, are examined instead. This section develops that examination and applies it to both worked examples.

4.1 Residuals

NoteDefinition: residual

The residual for observation \(i\) is the difference between the observed and the fitted outcome:

\[ e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i \]

It is the observable counterpart of the unobservable error, \(\epsilon_i = Y_i - E\{Y_i\}\), which is the deviation of the observation from the population regression line.

The distinction matters. The error measures distance from the true population line, which is never known. The residual measures distance from the fitted sample line, which is known. Residual analysis proceeds on the reasoning that if the model’s conditions hold, the residuals should behave approximately as a sample of independent, normally distributed values with constant variance and mean zero.

Two properties of least squares residuals follow from the estimation itself and are not evidence of anything: they sum to zero, and they are uncorrelated with the predictor. Diagnostic information lies in their pattern, not their sum.

Because residuals are measured in the units of the outcome, judging whether one is “large” requires a scale. Dividing a residual by its estimated standard deviation gives a standardised residual, a unitless quantity expressing how many standard deviations an observation lies from the fitted line. This makes a rough flag available: standardised residuals beyond \(\pm 2\) merit a look. That threshold should be used with care, since in well-behaved data roughly 5% of observations exceed it by chance alone; flagging only values beyond \(\pm 3\), where about 0.2% would be expected, is often more practical. In either case a flagged observation is marked for investigation, not for deletion.

4.2 Residuals versus fitted values

The residuals-versus-fitted-values plot is the most frequently produced diagnostic in regression. Residuals are plotted on the vertical axis against fitted values on the horizontal axis. Because any observation lying exactly on the regression line has a residual of zero, the horizontal line at zero in this plot is the fitted regression line, viewed edge-on.

TipReading a residuals versus fitted values plot

A well-behaved plot has three features:

  1. Residuals bounce randomly about the zero line — supporting linearity.
  2. Residuals form a roughly horizontal band of constant width — supporting equal variances.
  3. No residual stands out conspicuously from the rest — suggesting no outliers.

Figure 3 shows this plot for the regression of FBS on body mass index.

The plot fails two of the three criteria. The vertical spread of residuals is far from constant: it is narrow at low fitted values and widens substantially as fitted values increase. And the residuals are strongly asymmetric, reaching almost 23 mmol/L above the line but only about 5.2 mmol/L below it.

Both features are consequences of the outcome’s skew, noted in Section 3.1. Fasting blood sugar has a floor near zero but no practical ceiling, so participants with impaired glucose regulation generate large positive residuals with no negative counterparts. The equal-variance condition is not satisfied, and the normality condition is unlikely to be either.

A caution about reading such plots is warranted. Interpretation is subjective, and the temptation to see structure in randomness is strong — particularly in small datasets. The practical rule is that genuine problems announce themselves clearly; if a plot looks broadly acceptable, it usually is. The pattern in Figure 3 is not a subtle one.

4.3 Residuals versus the predictor

Residuals can also be plotted against a predictor. The criteria for reading the plot are exactly those of Section 4.2, but its purpose depends on which predictor is chosen.

If the predictor is already in the model, the plot adds nothing in simple linear regression. Fitted values are a linear function of the single predictor, so this plot is a rescaled version of Figure 3, horizontally stretched or reflected.

If the predictor is not in the model, the plot becomes genuinely informative, and this is where its value lies. Residuals may be regarded as a “new response” — the outcome after removing what the current model explains. Plotting this new response against a candidate predictor asks whether that variable explains any of the variation left over. A systematic trend indicates that it does and should be considered for inclusion; no trend indicates it need not be.

Figure 4 makes the case for multiple regression on diagnostic grounds rather than by assertion. Both omitted predictors show clear upward trends against the residuals, so both explain variation that body mass index alone does not. This observation motivates Section 5 directly.

4.4 Identifying specific problems from residual plots

Different violations leave different signatures. Table 5 summarises the mapping.

Two warnings apply to this table. First, a high \(R^2\) provides no protection against any of these problems: a model can explain the great majority of the variance in the outcome and still display unmistakable curvature in its residuals. Second, more than one problem can occur simultaneously, and frequently does. In Figure 3 the same plot shows both non-constant variance and marked asymmetry.

4.5 The normal probability plot of residuals

Equal variance and linearity are assessed from residual plots. Normality requires a different display: the normal probability plot, also called the quantile–quantile or QQ plot.

Its construction is a direct comparison of observed and expected quantiles. The residuals are ordered from smallest to largest. For each, the value that would be expected at that position in a sample of the same size from a normal distribution is computed. Observed values are plotted against expected values. Since the mean and variance of the errors are unknown, standardised residuals are used and the expected quantiles become standard normal scores. If the residuals are normally distributed, the points fall approximately on a straight line.

Four patterns recur, and recognising them is the point of the plot:

Pattern in the normal probability plot Interpretation
Points approximately on a straight line Normality is reasonable
Straight except for one or two deviating points Normality is reasonable apart from outliers, which should be investigated
A smooth curve, bending away from the line The residual distribution is skewed
Straight in the middle, departing at both ends The residual distribution is heavy-tailed

Figure 5 shows the third pattern unambiguously. The points follow the reference line through the central portion of the distribution and then curve steeply above it in the upper tail. The accompanying histogram confirms a long right tail. The residual distribution is skewed, not normal, with a skewness coefficient of 2.83 — a symmetric distribution would give approximately zero.

How much this matters depends on what is being estimated, following the sensitivity ordering set out in Section 3. Inference about the slope is comparatively robust to non-normality, and at 4295 observations the central limit theorem protects the confidence interval for \(b_1\) substantially. Prediction intervals for individual participants receive no such protection and would be unreliable here. The failure of equal variance seen in Figure 3 is the more serious of the two problems, because interval estimates and \(p\)-values are moderately sensitive to it.

4.6 Further residual plot examples

Diagnostic plots look different when the predictor is categorical, and the second worked example illustrates this.

The left panel of Figure 6 contains only two vertical stripes of points. This is not a defect: a two-level predictor generates exactly two fitted values, the two group means. The interpretive rules must be adapted accordingly. Curvature cannot be assessed at all, since two points always determine a straight line and the linearity condition is automatically satisfied for a binary predictor. What can be assessed is whether the two stripes have comparable vertical spread, which is the equal-variance condition in the form it takes here — the assumption of a two-sample \(t\)-test.

Here the two stripes are of similar length, and a formal test finds no evidence against constant variance (\(p\) = 0.345). This is an instructive contrast with Figure 3. The equal-variance condition can hold comfortably in one model and fail badly in another fitted to the same outcome, because what the condition concerns is whether residual spread changes across the fitted values — and a two-level predictor produces only two of them. Passing this check is therefore much less reassuring for a binary predictor than it would be for a continuous one. The normal probability plot in the right panel still shows pronounced right skew, which is expected: the skew belongs to the outcome, and changing the predictor does not remove it.

For completeness, the patterns to expect in other situations are worth naming, since they will not appear in this chapter’s data. A correctly specified model produces residuals of constant spread with no discernible pattern. A wrongly specified functional form produces curvature, often together with increasing variance, as two simultaneous problems. Heavy-tailed errors produce a normal probability plot that is straight in the middle and departs at both ends. And where curvature and non-constant variance occur together, transforming the outcome — for instance to \(\sqrt{y}\) — can sometimes resolve both at once, with predictions then squared back onto the original scale. That remedy is the subject of Section 7.

ImportantWhere this leaves the two simple models

Both models have markedly right-skewed residuals, and the body mass index model additionally has non-constant variance. The estimated slopes remain unbiased, and the substantive conclusions — a positive association with body mass index, a small negative difference for single participants — are unlikely to be artefacts. But for the body mass index model the standard errors, and therefore the confidence intervals and \(p\)-values, cannot be taken at face value.

Two responses are available, and both are pursued below: bring in additional predictors so that less variation is left unexplained (Section 5), and transform the variables so that the conditions are better satisfied (Section 7).

5 Multiple Linear Regression

The diagnostic evidence of Section 4.3 showed that variables omitted from the simple model explain variation the model leaves behind. There is also a more fundamental reason to move beyond one predictor. In observational health research the association between an exposure and an outcome is almost never the association of interest on its own, because the people who differ in exposure differ in other ways as well. Multiple linear regression is the standard tool for separating these influences.

5.1 From one predictor to several

Multiple linear regression extends simple linear regression to two or more predictors. The extension serves two distinct purposes, and confusing them is a frequent source of error.

The first is prediction. More predictors generally mean more of the outcome’s variation is explained and individual predictions become more accurate.

The second, and in epidemiology far more important, is adjustment. Suppose interest lies in whether body mass index is associated with fasting blood sugar. Participants with a higher body mass index are on average older, have higher blood pressure and have higher triglyceride concentrations. The crude association of Section 3.7.1 mixes all of these together. Multiple regression estimates the association attributable to body mass index among participants who are alike in the other measured variables — the partial or adjusted association.

TipThe meaning, and the limits, of “holding other variables constant”

An adjusted coefficient is routinely described as the effect of a predictor “holding the other predictors constant”. The phrase is accurate about the arithmetic and misleading about the science. It describes a statistical comparison between participants with identical values of the other predictors in the model. It does not mean the variable has been experimentally manipulated, and it does not extend to variables that were never measured. Adjustment removes confounding by the covariates in the model, and by nothing else.

5.2 The multiple linear regression model

NoteThe multiple linear regression model

With \(k\) predictors,

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik} + \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2) \ \text{independently} \]

where \(\beta_0\) is the mean outcome when every predictor equals zero, and each \(\beta_j\) is the change in the mean outcome per one-unit increase in \(x_j\) with all other predictors held constant. The corresponding regression function is

\[ E\{Y_i\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_k x_{ik} \]

Three points about this model deserve emphasis.

“Linear” still refers to the parameters. The predictors may include squares, logarithms or products of other predictors, and the model remains a linear model. This is what permits the transformations of Section 7 and the interaction terms of Section 8 to be handled without leaving the framework.

The geometry generalises. With one predictor the fitted model is a line; with two it is a plane; with more than two it is a hyperplane that cannot be visualised but is described by exactly the same algebra.

The error variance estimate changes its divisor. With \(k\) predictors, \(k+1\) parameters are estimated, so

\[ \hat{\sigma}^2 = \text{MSE} = \frac{SSE}{n - (k+1)} \]

The sums-of-squares partition \(SST = SSR + SSE\) carries over unchanged, and so does \(R^2 = SSR/SST\), now called the coefficient of multiple determination. Because \(R^2\) cannot decrease when a predictor is added, the adjusted \(R^2\) is used to compare models of different sizes:

\[ R^2_{adj} = 1 - \left( \frac{n-1}{n - (k+1)} \right) (1 - R^2) \]

Unlike \(R^2\), the adjusted version can fall when a predictor contributes less than its degree of freedom costs, which makes it the appropriate quantity for comparing competing models. It plays exactly that role in Section 7.

5.2.1 Categorical predictors and indicator variables

A categorical predictor with more than two levels cannot enter the model as a single number, because its codes carry no numerical meaning. It is represented instead by a set of indicator (dummy) variables: for a variable with \(c\) levels, \(c-1\) indicators are required, and the omitted level becomes the reference category.

Ethnicity in the MSSM dataset has four levels, so three indicators are needed. Taking Malay as the reference:

\[ x_{\text{Chinese}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Chinese} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad x_{\text{Indian}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Indian} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad x_{\text{Other}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if Other} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

A Malay participant has all three indicators equal to zero, so the reference category is absorbed into the intercept. Each of the three coefficients is then the difference in mean outcome between that ethnic group and the Malay group, adjusted for the remaining covariates. The choice of reference category changes the coefficients but changes nothing substantive — no fitted value, no \(R^2\), and no overall test result depends on it. It is chosen for interpretability, and the largest or most clinically natural group is the usual choice.

5.3 Fitting the multivariable model

The model carried through the remainder of this chapter regresses fasting blood sugar on nine covariates: place of residence, ethnicity, age, body mass index, waist–hip ratio, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol, fasting triglyceride, and history of diabetes.

Adiposity is represented by the two derived indices of Section 3.1.1 rather than by waist circumference. The reason is that waist circumference overlaps heavily with both — it is correlated 0.80 with body mass index and, being the numerator of the waist–hip ratio, 0.67 with that. Entering all three would ask the model to separate three measurements of largely the same thing. Section 5.6 fits exactly that model and shows what goes wrong. Using BMI and WHR together, by contrast, captures overall and central adiposity as two nearly independent dimensions.

Table 6 reports the result.

The model was fitted to 4291 participants with complete data on all ten variables, 4 records having been excluded. It explains \(R^2 = 30.6\)% of the variation in fasting blood sugar, with an adjusted \(R^2\) of 30.4% — a substantial improvement on the 2.2% achieved by body mass index alone, and a direct vindication of the diagnostic signal in Figure 4. The residual standard error has fallen from 2.54 to 2.15 mmol/L.

The fitted regression equation, written out in full, is

\[ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{FBS}} = & 2.653 + 0.134 \, (\text{urban}) -0.592 \, (\text{Chinese}) \\ & -0.028 \, (\text{Indian}) -1.490 \, (\text{Other}) + 0.0034 \, \text{age} \\ & + 0.0153 \, \text{BMI} + 0.2721 \, \text{WHR} + 0.0043 \, \text{SBP} \\ & + 0.163 \, \text{cholesterol} + 0.350 \, \text{triglyceride} + 3.313 \, (\text{diabetes history}) \end{aligned} \]

Three coefficients illustrate how such a model is read.

A continuous covariate. The coefficient for fasting triglyceride is 0.350 mmol/L (95% CI 0.285 to 0.416, \(p\) < 0.001). Among participants of the same residence, ethnicity, age, body mass index, waist–hip ratio, systolic blood pressure, total cholesterol and diabetes history, a triglyceride concentration higher by 1 mmol/L is associated with a mean fasting blood sugar higher by 0.350 mmol/L.

A derived covariate on an awkward scale. The coefficient for waist–hip ratio is 0.272 mmol/L (95% CI -0.339 to 0.883, \(p\) 0.383). Read literally this is the change in mean FBS for a one-unit increase in the ratio — but WHR spans only 0.59 to 1.58, so a one-unit change is far larger than anything observed. A ratio is best rescaled before reporting: per 0.1 higher WHR, roughly the gap between the first and third quartiles of this sample, mean FBS differs by 0.0272 mmol/L. Whenever a coefficient’s natural unit is much larger than the spread of the variable, rescale it before reporting.

A categorical covariate. The coefficient for history of diabetes is 3.313 mmol/L (95% CI 3.098 to 3.528). Adjusted for the other seven covariates, participants reporting a previous diagnosis of diabetes have a mean fasting blood sugar 3.313 mmol/L higher than those who do not. As noted in Section 3.7, this is a marker of established disease rather than a risk factor, and it is in the model to make the other coefficients interpretable rather than to be interpreted itself.

5.4 Crude and adjusted estimates compared

The purpose of adjustment is best seen by placing crude and adjusted estimates side by side, as in Table 7.

Every association is attenuated by adjustment, which is the expected consequence of covariates that are correlated with one another and with the outcome. The attenuation is severe for the adiposity measures: body mass index falls from 0.0738 to 0.0153 mmol/L per kg/m², and waist–hip ratio from 2.693 to 0.272, the latter losing statistical significance entirely (\(p\) 0.383). Most of what the crude adiposity associations captured is shared with triglyceride, blood pressure and diabetes status — which is precisely what one would expect of the metabolic syndrome this study was designed to examine.

One result, however, is qualitatively different and is the most instructive finding in this chapter.

ImportantAdjustment can eliminate an association entirely

Considered alone, age is strongly associated with fasting blood sugar: 0.0335 mmol/L per year of age, with \(p\) = 6.9 × 10-36. It appeared in Table 2 as one of the more convincing covariates.

Adjusted for the other seven covariates, the age coefficient falls to 0.0034 mmol/L per year with a 95% confidence interval of -0.0019 to 0.0087 and \(p\) = 0.213. The association has disappeared.

The explanation is not that age is unimportant, but that its crude association operates through the other measured variables. Older participants in this sample have a higher body mass index, higher systolic blood pressure and a much higher prevalence of diagnosed diabetes. Once participants are compared within strata of those variables, age itself adds essentially nothing.

Whether that is the right analysis depends entirely on the research question, and this is a subject-matter judgement rather than a statistical one:

  • If the question is how much fasting blood sugar differs between older and younger people in this population, the crude estimate answers it, and adjusting away the pathways through which age acts would be a mistake.
  • If the question is whether age has an influence on glycaemia beyond its effects on adiposity, blood pressure and diabetes status, the adjusted estimate answers it, and the answer is that it does not detectably.

The distinction is the classical one between confounders and mediators. A confounder is a common cause of exposure and outcome, and adjusting for it removes bias. A mediator lies on the causal pathway from exposure to outcome, and adjusting for it removes part of the very effect being estimated. The two are statistically indistinguishable — both change the coefficient when added to a model — and can be separated only by reasoning about the subject matter and the temporal ordering of the variables. Body mass index and diabetes status are far more plausibly consequences of ageing than causes of it, which suggests that here the adjusted age coefficient has removed mediated effects rather than confounding.

5.5 Testing several parameters at once: the general linear F-test

Table 6 reports a \(t\)-test for each coefficient, each of which asks whether a single parameter is zero. Some questions cannot be phrased that way. Ethnicity occupies three coefficients, and “does ethnicity matter?” is a question about all three simultaneously. Testing them one at a time is both indirect and statistically wasteful, since performing several tests inflates the chance of a spurious result.

The general linear F-test answers such questions with a single test. Its logic is a comparison of two nested models:

  1. Specify a full model containing all the parameters of interest.
  2. Specify a reduced model obtained by imposing the constraint stated in the null hypothesis — here, that all three ethnicity coefficients are zero.
  3. Compare the two models’ error sums of squares.
NoteThe general linear F-test

\[ F^* = \frac{\left( SSE(R) - SSE(F) \right) / \left( df_R - df_F \right)}{SSE(F) / df_F} \]

where \(SSE(R)\) and \(SSE(F)\) are the error sums of squares of the reduced and full models, and \(df_R\) and \(df_F\) are their error degrees of freedom. The null hypothesis always corresponds to the reduced model and the alternative to the full model. A large \(F^*\), and correspondingly small \(p\)-value, rejects the reduced model in favour of the full one.

Because the reduced model is constrained, it can never fit better than the full model, so \(SSE(R) \ge SSE(F)\) always. The test asks whether the improvement in fit is larger than the extra parameters would be expected to deliver by chance alone.

5.5.1 Application: does ethnicity contribute to the model?

The hypotheses are

\[ H_0: \beta_{\text{Chinese}} = \beta_{\text{Indian}} = \beta_{\text{Other}} = 0 \qquad \text{versus} \qquad H_A: \text{at least one is non-zero} \]

Fitting both models to the same 4291 participants gives \(SSE(R) = 20830.5\) with \(df_R = 4282\), and \(SSE(F) = 19699.8\) with \(df_F = 4279\). Substituting into the formula:

\[ F^* = \frac{(20830.5 - 19699.8) / (4282 - 4279)} {19699.8 / 4279} = \frac{376.9}{4.6038} = 81.87 \]

With 3 and 4279 degrees of freedom this gives \(p\) < 0.001. The reduced model is rejected: ethnicity contributes to the explanation of fasting blood sugar after adjustment for the other seven covariates.

This conclusion could not have been drawn safely from Table 6, where the Indian-versus-Malay contrast is not significant (\(p\) = 0.821) while the other two are. Individual contrasts answer questions about specific group comparisons; the F-test answers the question about the variable as a whole. The F-test is also invariant to the choice of reference category, whereas the individual \(t\)-tests are not — another reason to prefer it for this purpose.

Two special cases of the same test are worth recognising. When the reduced model contains only the intercept, the general linear F-test becomes the overall F-test reported with every regression output, testing whether all slopes are simultaneously zero; here it gives \(F\) = 171.5 on 11 and 4279 degrees of freedom, \(p\) < 0.001. When the reduced model omits exactly one parameter, the F-test is algebraically equivalent to the \(t\)-test for that coefficient, since \(t^2 = F\) on one numerator degree of freedom. The general form is needed only for testing a subset of two or more parameters.

5.6 Multicollinearity

Adjustment relies on being able to separate the contributions of correlated predictors. When predictors are highly correlated with one another, that separation becomes unstable — a condition called multicollinearity. Its symptoms are inflated standard errors, coefficients that change substantially when a covariate is added or removed, and occasionally coefficients with implausible signs.

The variance inflation factor (VIF) quantifies it: \(\text{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2)\), where \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing predictor \(j\) on all the others. A VIF of 1 indicates no correlation with the other predictors; values above 5 are commonly regarded as cause for concern and values above 10 as serious. For multi-category variables the generalised VIF is reported, and is compared after taking the root indicated by its degrees of freedom.

Table 8 is reassuring: every value is close to 1, the largest being 1.44. The nine covariates carry largely distinct information, and the adjusted coefficients can be interpreted without concern on this count. Body mass index and waist–hip ratio coexist comfortably because, as Section 3.1.1 showed, they measure different things and are correlated only 0.24.

5.6.1 What multicollinearity looks like when it is present

This model was constructed to avoid the problem, and a reader could be forgiven for concluding that multicollinearity is a theoretical worry. It is not. The dataset makes it easy to demonstrate: simply add waist circumference back alongside body mass index and waist–hip ratio, so that three overlapping measures of adiposity compete to explain the same variation.

The consequences are textbook, and every one of them is visible above.

The variance inflation factors rise sharply, but only for the affected terms. Waist circumference reaches 8.5, body mass index 5.0 and waist–hip ratio 3.3, all beyond the conventional threshold of 5. Meanwhile residence, ethnicity, age, blood pressure, cholesterol, triglyceride and diabetes history are essentially unchanged from Table 8. Multicollinearity is a local problem: it damages the estimates of the variables involved and leaves the rest of the model alone.

The standard errors inflate. The standard error of the body mass index coefficient increases by a factor of 2.06 — the “variance inflation” the statistic is named for. This is the mechanism by which collinearity does its damage.

Significance evaporates. In Table 6 body mass index was significant at \(p\) 0.026. With waist circumference added, all three adiposity terms become non-significant (\(p\) = 0.38, 0.75 and 0.82). A naive reading would conclude that adiposity is unrelated to fasting blood sugar, which is plainly false — the three measures are simply unable to be told apart.

Yet the model as a whole fits no better. The general linear F-test for adding waist circumference gives \(F\) = 0.05 on 1 and 4278 degrees of freedom, \(p\) = 0.82, and the adjusted \(R^2\) actually falls slightly, from 30.415% to 30.399%. Waist circumference contributes nothing that BMI and WHR have not already contributed; it merely makes the existing coefficients harder to estimate.

WarningRecognising and handling multicollinearity

The signature is a combination that should always prompt suspicion: a model that fits well overall while few or none of its individual predictors are significant, often accompanied by coefficients that change substantially — sometimes reversing sign — when a covariate is added or removed.

Detection: inspect pairwise correlations among predictors before fitting, and compute the VIF afterwards. Values above 5 warrant attention, above 10 are serious. As a rule of thumb, avoid entering predictors correlated above about 0.7 into the same model; here waist circumference correlates 0.80 with BMI.

Remedies, in the order usually worth trying: choose one measure from each correlated group on subject-matter grounds, which is what Table 6 does; combine the correlated variables into a single index, which is what BMI and WHR already are; or centre the predictors, which helps specifically for the collinearity between a variable and its own square or product term (Section 8).

What multicollinearity does not do is bias the coefficients or damage the model’s predictions. If prediction is the sole aim, it can be ignored. It matters when the goal is to interpret individual coefficients — which, in epidemiology, it usually is.

The dataset offers other opportunities to create the same problem. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure are correlated 0.69, and weight, hip circumference and neck circumference are all closely related to the adiposity measures already in the model. Entering several members of any of these groups together would reproduce the instability shown above.

The model is now fitted, its coefficients interpreted, its ethnicity block tested and its predictors checked for redundancy. What has not been examined is whether the conditions underlying all of these inferences are satisfied.

6 Assessment of Multiple Linear Regression

Every quantity in Table 6 — each standard error, each confidence interval, each \(p\)-value, and the F-test of Section 5.5 — was computed on the assumption that the model’s conditions hold. This section states those conditions for the multivariable case, assesses them graphically, and then applies the formal tests for the two that are most often examined in practice.

6.1 The assumptions for multiple linear regression

The LINE conditions of Section 3 carry over directly. The only change is that “at each value of \(x\)” becomes “at each set of values of the predictors”.

NoteThe LINE conditions for multiple linear regression

For each combination of predictor values \((x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{ik})\):

Condition Statement
L Linear The mean outcome is a linear function of the predictors
I Independent The errors are independent of one another
N Normal The errors are normally distributed
E Equal variance The errors have the same variance \(\sigma^2\)

Equivalently, the errors are independent \(N(0, \sigma^2)\) random variables. Two further conditions are implicit: the predictor values are treated as fixed and measured without error, and the model is correctly specified, containing the variables that matter in the form in which they matter.

A word on each condition as it applies to the model of Section 5.3.

Linearity is now a statement about each predictor’s contribution, holding the others fixed. It could fail for one predictor while holding for the rest — for instance if fasting blood sugar rose with age up to a point and then levelled off. It is assessed one predictor at a time.

Independence requires that no observation’s error conveys information about another’s. It typically fails by design rather than by accident, in three recognisable situations: repeated measurements taken on the same individual over time; naturally grouped data, such as pupils within schools or patients within clinics, where members of a group resemble one another; and data collected in a time or spatial sequence, where neighbouring observations are correlated. None of these applies to the MSSM data, where each record is a separate participant measured once, so the condition is satisfied here. Where it does not hold, the remedy is not a repair to the linear model but a different class of model — mixed-effects models for grouped data, time-series models for sequential data. Independence deserves this attention because, as noted in Section 3, inference is very sensitive to its failure, and no residual plot will reveal a violation that the study design has built in.

Normality concerns the errors, not the outcome or the predictors. It is common to see the outcome’s own distribution tested for normality before fitting a regression; this is not what the model requires. A markedly skewed outcome can still yield well-behaved residuals if the skew is explained by the predictors.

Equal variance, or homoscedasticity, requires the scatter of errors to be the same everywhere. Its failure does not bias the coefficients, but it invalidates the standard errors and therefore everything computed from them.

6.2 Assessing the model assumptions

All the diagnostic tools of Section 4 apply unchanged. Figure 7 shows the standard set for the multivariable model.

The four panels tell a consistent story, and it is the same story as in Section 4.

The residuals-versus-fitted plot shows a clear fan: residual spread is narrow where fitted values are low and much wider where they are high. Equal variance fails. The scale-location plot, which plots the square root of the absolute standardised residual against the fitted value, makes the same point more directly — a horizontal smoother would indicate constant variance, and this one rises steadily. The normal probability plot follows the reference line through the centre and then departs sharply upward, the signature of right skew described in Section 4.5. The histogram confirms it: residual skewness is 2.54 and kurtosis is 15.3, against values of 0 and 3 for a normal distribution.

Linearity is assessed predictor by predictor, in Figure 8.

These panels are more encouraging. Each smoother is close to horizontal across the region where most of the data lie, so the linear specification of each predictor is adequate; the problems in this model concern the error distribution, not the functional form. This distinction matters for Section 7, because it determines which transformation is worth attempting.

A final graphical check plots the residuals against predictors omitted from the model, asking whether an important variable has been left out.

Neither omitted variable shows a marked trend in Figure 9, so neither is an obviously missing predictor. This is expected, since each is closely related to variables already included. The waist circumference panel is the graphical counterpart of the formal test in Section 5.6.1: the flat smoother says there is no leftover signal for waist circumference to explain, which is why adding it inflated the standard errors without improving the fit.

6.2.1 Outliers, leverage and influence

Three related but distinct ideas arise when individual observations are examined.

  • An outlier has a large residual: its outcome is far from what the model predicts.
  • A high-leverage point has an unusual combination of predictor values, far from the centre of the predictor space. Leverage concerns the \(x\) values only and can be computed before the outcome is even seen.
  • An influential point is one whose removal would materially change the fitted model. Influence combines the other two: a point that is both an outlier and high-leverage is the classic influential observation.

Conventional diagnostics and thresholds are as follows, with the values for this model shown.

Diagnostic What it measures Conventional threshold This model
Standardised residual How many SDs an observation lies from the fitted value \(\vert e^* \vert > 2\) (or \(> 3\)) 205 of 4291 (4.8%)
Leverage \(h_{ii}\) How unusual the predictor values are \((2k+2)/n\) = 0.0056 222 above
Cook’s distance Combined effect of residual and leverage on the fit \(4/n\) = 0.0009 269 above; maximum 0.036
DFBETA Change in one coefficient when the observation is deleted Context-dependent —

The picture is reassuring despite the counts. The proportion of standardised residuals beyond \(\pm 2\) is 4.8%, almost exactly the 5% expected by chance under a correct model. More importantly, the largest Cook’s distance is 0.036, far below 1 and only a few multiples of the \(4/n\) threshold. No single participant exerts material influence over the fitted model. This is a common and comfortable situation in large datasets: with 4291 observations, no one record can dominate. In small studies the same diagnostics frequently identify one or two observations that change the conclusions entirely, which is why they should always be inspected. Observations flagged this way are candidates for investigation, never for automatic deletion.

6.3 Tests for error normality

Graphical assessment can be supplemented by formal tests. All share the same hypotheses:

\[ H_0: \text{the errors follow a normal distribution} \qquad H_A: \text{the errors do not follow a normal distribution} \]

Note the direction: a large \(p\)-value is the favourable outcome, since it means the normality hypothesis is not rejected. Four tests are in common use.

Test Basis
Anderson–Darling Measures the squared area between the empirical distribution of the residuals and the fitted normal cumulative distribution, weighted to give extra emphasis to the tails. Smaller \(A^2\) indicates better agreement.
Shapiro–Wilk Compares the ordered residuals with the values expected from a normal sample, forming a ratio \(W\) that approaches 1 under normality. Small \(W\) leads to rejection.
Ryan–Joiner A simpler correlation-based alternative to Shapiro–Wilk: the correlation \(R_p\) between the ordered residuals and their normal scores. Values near 1 indicate normality.
Kolmogorov–Smirnov (the Lilliefors test when parameters are estimated) Takes the largest vertical distance \(D\) between the empirical and the normal cumulative distribution functions.

Applied to the residuals of the multivariable model, the Shapiro–Wilk test gives \(W\) = 0.7836 with \(p\) < 0.001, and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test gives \(D\) = 0.1717 with \(p\) < 0.001. Both reject normality decisively, agreeing with Figure 7.

WarningNormality tests in large samples

These tests should not be given more weight than they deserve. Their power increases with sample size, so in large datasets they reject normality for departures far too small to affect any conclusion. With 4291 observations, essentially no real dataset will pass. A significant result therefore establishes that the residuals are non-normal, but says nothing about how much it matters.

The practical rule is that plots lead and tests corroborate. Here the plots show substantial right skew, not a trivial departure, so the test result reflects something real. Had the normal probability plot looked straight, a significant Shapiro–Wilk test at this sample size would have warranted no action at all.

The consequences follow the sensitivity ordering of Section 3. Inference about the regression coefficients is fairly robust to non-normality, and at this sample size the central limit theorem makes the confidence intervals in Table 6 broadly trustworthy on this count. Prediction intervals for individual participants are not robust and should not be used from this model.

6.4 Tests for constant error variance

The second condition to be tested formally is equal variance. The hypotheses are

\[ H_0: \text{the error variance is constant} \qquad H_A: \text{the error variance is not constant} \]

and again a large \(p\)-value is the favourable outcome. Several tests are available, most of which work by dividing the residuals into \(g \ge 2\) groups — commonly by low versus high fitted values — and comparing variability between them.

Test Basis and requirements
F-test Splits residuals into two groups by predictor value and compares their variances directly through \(F^* = s_1^2 / s_2^2\). Requires normal errors.
Modified Levene, also called the Brown–Forsythe test Compares the mean absolute deviation of residuals from their group median across groups. Being based on medians it is nonparametric and does not require normal errors, which makes it the robust choice.
Breusch–Pagan, also called the Cook–Weisberg score test Regresses the squared residuals on the predictors and tests whether that relationship is flat. Assumes normal errors.
Bartlett’s test Compares group variances through a pooled-variance statistic. Highly sensitive to non-normality; Levene’s test is preferred when normality is in doubt.

The Breusch–Pagan test gives \(\chi^2\) = 339.7 on 11 degrees of freedom, \(p\) < 0.001.

The modified Levene (Brown–Forsythe) test, dividing the residuals into quartiles of fitted value, gives \(F\) = 150.8 on 3 and 4287 degrees of freedom, \(p\) < 0.001.

Both reject the constant-variance hypothesis emphatically, and here the two tests reinforce one another usefully: Breusch–Pagan assumes normal errors, which has just been shown to fail, but Brown–Forsythe does not require normality and reaches the same conclusion. The failure is not an artefact of the normality violation.

The magnitude is easy to see directly. Residual standard deviations across quartiles of fitted value are 1.45, 1.52, 1.73, 3.31 mmol/L — the most variable quartile has roughly 2.3 times the spread of the least. This is a large departure, not a marginal one.

ImportantWhat the diagnostics establish, and what follows

The multivariable model has adequate linearity for every predictor (Figure 8), no influential observations (Section 6.2), and no multicollinearity (Section 5.6). Independence holds by design. But the errors are not normally distributed and, more seriously, their variance is not constant.

The practical consequence is specific. The coefficients in Table 6 remain unbiased estimates — heteroscedasticity does not bias \(b\). What is unreliable is their precision: the standard errors, and therefore the confidence intervals and \(p\)-values, are computed under an assumption the data contradict.

Two remedies are standard. The first is to transform a variable so that the conditions are better met, which is the subject of Section 7. The second is to keep the model and compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors, which are valid without the equal-variance assumption. Both are legitimate; the first changes the model, the second changes only the inference drawn from it.

7 Transformation
