Section 6 left the multivariable model with two failed conditions. Transformation — re-expressing a predictor or the outcome on a different scale — is the classical remedy. Because a “linear” model requires linearity only in the parameters (Section 5.2), a model fitted to transformed variables is still a linear model, and all the machinery of the preceding sections continues to apply.

This section covers when to transform a predictor, what other transformations are available, and what happens when they are applied to these data. The results are instructive precisely because they are mixed.

7.1 Log-transforming a predictor

The natural logarithm compresses large values and spreads out small ones. Applied to a predictor, it changes the shape of that predictor’s relationship with the outcome without touching the outcome’s error distribution.

TipWhen to consider log-transforming a predictor

Transforming a predictor is the appropriate first remedy when non-linearity is the only problem — when independence, normality and equal variance are already satisfactory. Specific indications are:

  1. The residuals-versus-predictor plot is curved, with the outcome rising steeply at low predictor values and flattening at high ones.
  2. The predictor is strongly right-skewed, so that a few large values exert disproportionate leverage.
  3. The predictor plausibly acts multiplicatively rather than additively — that is, proportional rather than absolute changes are what matter biologically.
  4. The predictor spans several orders of magnitude.

Two constraints apply. The logarithm is undefined at zero and for negative values, so a strictly positive predictor is required. And transformation is iterative: conditions satisfied before a transformation may fail after it, so the diagnostics must be re-checked each time.

Interpretation changes in a way that must be handled carefully. With a predictor on the log scale, the coefficient is no longer a change per unit of the predictor but a change per multiplicative change. Using \(\log_2\) rather than \(\log_e\) makes this directly readable: the coefficient becomes the change in mean outcome associated with a doubling of the predictor.

7.1.1 Application to fasting triglyceride

Among the continuous covariates in the model, fasting triglyceride is the most strongly right-skewed, with a skewness coefficient of 3.18 and values from 0.11 to 12.66 mmol/L. It is also conventionally log-transformed in the lipid literature. It is therefore the natural candidate.

Figure 10 confirms that the transformation does what it is supposed to do to the predictor’s own distribution. Table 11 compares the two models.

The coefficient on the log scale is 0.439 mmol/L (95% CI 0.342 to 0.535), meaning that a doubling of fasting triglyceride is associated with a mean fasting blood sugar higher by 0.439 mmol/L, adjusted for the other covariates. That is an interpretable and clinically communicable statement.

ImportantThe transformation does not improve this model

Despite the strong skew that motivated it, log-transforming triglyceride makes the model slightly worse. Adjusted \(R^2\) falls from 30.41% to 29.92%, the residual standard error rises from 2.146 to 2.153 mmol/L, and AIC rises by 30.3 points. On every criterion the untransformed model fits marginally better.

This is not a failure of the analysis but an illustration of an important principle. A skewed predictor is not by itself a reason to transform. The diagnostics in Figure 8 showed that the linear specification of triglyceride was already adequate — the smoother was essentially flat. There was no non-linearity to fix, so the transformation had nothing to repair, and it slightly degraded a relationship that was already close to linear.

The rule that follows is: transform in response to a diagnosed problem, not in response to a distribution. Had these two models been compared only on \(R^2\), with the transformation adopted or rejected on that basis, the reasoning would have been backwards. The choice between them here should rest on interpretability — and “per doubling” may well be preferable to “per mmol/L” for communicating to a clinical audience, at a negligible cost in fit.

7.2 Other transformations

Log-transforming a predictor is one option among many. The main alternatives are summarised below.

Transformation Form Typical use
Log of predictor \(\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x\) Outcome rises steeply then flattens; right-skewed predictor
Log of outcome \(\mu_{\ln Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) Right-skewed outcome; variance growing with the mean
Log of both \(\mu_{\ln Y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \ln x\) Multiplicative relationships; coefficient becomes an elasticity
Reciprocal \(\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1/x)\) Outcome approaching an asymptote
Exponential \(\mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 e^{-x}\) Decay relationships
Square root \(y^* = \sqrt{y}\) Count outcomes; variance proportional to the mean
Arcsine \(\hat{p}^* = \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{\hat{p}})\) Proportions (largely superseded by logistic regression)
Power / Box–Cox \(y^* = y^{\lambda}\) General-purpose variance stabilisation, \(\lambda\) estimated from the data

Two of these deserve comment. The square-root and arcsine transformations were historically the standard treatment for counts and proportions, but Poisson and logistic regression now handle those outcomes directly and are usually preferable. The Box–Cox procedure provides a systematic way to select a power transformation of the outcome, estimating \(\lambda\) by maximum likelihood over a range such as \([-2, 2]\); \(\lambda = 1\) means no transformation, \(\lambda = 0.5\) the square root, \(\lambda = 0\) the logarithm, and \(\lambda = -1\) the reciprocal. Values close to a recognisable transformation are conventionally rounded to it for interpretability.

Choosing among these remains partly trial and error. Two pieces of advice apply generally: do not delete observations merely to make a transformation work, and prefer some loss of fit over the loss of a clearly interpretable model, reporting the choice either way.

7.2.1 Transforming the outcome

The diagnostics of Section 6 pointed to a problem with the error distribution rather than with any predictor’s functional form: right-skewed residuals whose variance grows with the fitted value. That combination is the classic indication for transforming the outcome.

The Box–Cox procedure applied to this model estimates \(\hat{\lambda}\) = -0.15, close enough to zero to justify the logarithmic transformation, which is also the more interpretable choice. Table 12 and Figure 11 compare the models before and after.

The improvement in the residual distribution is substantial. Residual skewness falls from 2.54 to 0.36, and the Shapiro–Wilk statistic rises from 0.784 to 0.938. The normal probability plot in Figure 11 is far closer to a straight line, and adjusted \(R^2\) on the log scale is 35.2%.

ImportantThe transformation helps substantially but does not fix the problem

Both formal tests still reject decisively: Shapiro–Wilk \(p\) < 0.001 and Breusch–Pagan \(p\) < 0.001. Figure 11 shows why — the residual spread still widens with the fitted value, less dramatically than before but visibly.

It would be easy, and wrong, to present the log transformation as having solved the problem. It has improved matters considerably and has not resolved them. Reporting a transformed model without re-examining its diagnostics is a common error, and it is precisely the iterative re-checking urged in Section 7.1 that catches it.

Where does that leave the analysis? Three defensible positions, in increasing order of effort:

  1. Keep the untransformed model and use heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. The coefficients keep their direct mmol/L interpretation, and the inference no longer depends on the equal-variance assumption.
  2. Use the log-transformed model, accepting the change of interpretation and the residual imperfection, and report the diagnostics honestly.
  3. Use a model designed for a skewed positive outcome, such as a gamma regression with a log link, which specifies a mean–variance relationship appropriate to the data rather than requiring a transformation to manufacture one.

Interpretation on the log scale is worth stating explicitly, since it changes from additive to multiplicative. Exponentiating a coefficient converts it into a ratio of geometric means. For history of diabetes, the coefficient of 0.410 gives \(e^{0.410}\) = 1.507, so participants with a diabetes history have a geometric mean fasting blood sugar about 51% higher than those without, adjusted for the other covariates. Note that back-transforming the fitted values by exponentiating gives geometric rather than arithmetic means, which are systematically lower; this is a well-known trap when predictions are required on the original scale.

7.3 Generalized additive models

Transformation addresses non-linearity by requiring the analyst to choose a functional form — a logarithm, a square root, a reciprocal — and then imposing it. Generalized additive models (GAMs) take a different approach: they let the data determine the shape.

A GAM replaces the linear term \(\beta_j x_j\) with a smooth function \(f_j(x_j)\) estimated from the data:

\[ g\left( E\{Y\} \right) = \beta_0 + f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k) \]

where \(g\) is a link function, equal to the identity for a continuous outcome of the kind modelled in this chapter. Each \(f_j\) is typically built from splines, and its wiggliness is controlled by a penalty chosen automatically, usually by cross-validation or restricted maximum likelihood. A linear term is a special case: where the data support a straight line, the fitted smooth is a straight line.

TipStrengths of GAMs over multiple linear regression
  1. The shape of the exposure–outcome relationship is estimated, not assumed. This matters in epidemiology, where dose–response shape is often the scientific question.
  2. Continuous exposures need not be categorised. Splitting a continuous variable into quartiles to accommodate non-linearity discards information and reduces power; a smooth term avoids the compromise entirely.
  3. Non-monotone and threshold relationships can be captured — J-shaped and U-shaped associations, common for blood pressure, body mass index and many biomarkers, which no single transformation represents well.
  4. The degree of smoothing is chosen by the fitting procedure, through a penalty on wiggliness, rather than by the analyst inspecting plots and choosing a polynomial degree.
  5. Additivity is retained, so each covariate’s contribution can still be examined and plotted one at a time. A GAM is far more interpretable than a fully non-parametric model.

The costs should be stated as plainly as the benefits. There is no single coefficient to report for a smoothed covariate — the result is a curve, conveyed by a plot and an effective-degrees-of-freedom value, which is harder to tabulate and to communicate to non-statistical audiences. Flexible models can overfit, following features of the sample that will not replicate. And where a linear term is adequate, as Figure 8 indicates is the case for every predictor in this chapter’s model, a GAM adds complexity without adding insight.

In R, GAMs are fitted with the gam() function of the mgcv package, using terms of the form s(age) to request a smooth. Readers whose diagnostics show genuine curvature that no simple transformation resolves should regard GAMs as the natural next step.

8 Interaction

Every model fitted so far has made an assumption so quietly that it has not yet been stated: that each covariate’s association with fasting blood sugar is the same for everyone. The coefficient for age in Table 6 is a single number, applied identically to men and women, to rural and urban participants, and to those with and without diabetes. This section examines that assumption, and shows that in these data it is wrong.

8.1 Additive effects

NoteDefinition: additive effects

Two predictors have additive effects when the response function can be written as a sum of separate functions of each predictor:

\[ \mu_Y = f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k) \]

The effect of each predictor on the mean outcome is then the same regardless of the values taken by the others.

The first-order model \(y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \epsilon_i\) is additive by construction. Its geometry is best seen with one continuous and one binary predictor. Writing \(x_2 = 0\) and \(x_2 = 1\) for the two groups:

\[ \text{Group } x_2 = 0: \quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 \] \[ \text{Group } x_2 = 1: \quad \mu_Y = (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + \beta_1 x_1 \]

The two lines have the same slope \(\beta_1\) and differ only in their intercepts, by the constant amount \(\beta_2\).

TipThe visual signature of additivity is parallel lines

Under an additive model, the fitted lines for different groups are exactly parallel. The vertical distance between them, \(\beta_2\), is constant at every value of \(x_1\) — so a single number describes the group difference, and a single slope describes the effect of \(x_1\) in both groups.

Figure 12 shows what the additive model of Table 6 implies for the relationship between age and fasting blood sugar in participants with and without a history of diabetes.

The parallelism in Figure 12 is not a finding. It is an assumption, imposed by a model that contains no term permitting the slopes to differ. Whether the data support it is a separate question.

8.2 Multiplicative effects and interaction

NoteDefinition: interaction

Two predictors interact when the effect of one on the outcome depends on the value of the other. Equivalently, the response function is not additive — it cannot be written as a sum of separate functions of each predictor:

\[ \mu_Y \ne f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2) + \cdots + f_k(x_k) \]

Interaction is introduced into a linear model by including the product of the two predictors as an additional term:

\[ y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \beta_3 x_{i1} x_{i2} + \epsilon_i \]

The product \(x_{i1} x_{i2}\) is the two-way interaction term. The model remains a linear model — setting \(x_{i3} = x_{i1}x_{i2}\) recovers the standard three-predictor form — which is why interaction requires no new estimation theory.

To see what the product term does, separate the group-specific equations as before:

\[ \text{Group } x_2 = 0: \quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 \] \[ \text{Group } x_2 = 1: \quad \mu_Y = (\beta_0 + \beta_2) + (\beta_1 + \beta_3) x_1 \]

Now the lines differ in both intercept and slope. The interaction coefficient \(\beta_3\) is precisely the difference between the two groups’ slopes. Non-parallel lines are the visual signature of interaction, exactly as parallel lines are the signature of additivity.

The same logic applies when both predictors are continuous. For \(E\{Y\} = 10 + 2x_1 + 5x_2 + 0.5 x_1 x_2\), the slope with respect to \(x_1\) is \(2 + 0.5x_2\), which depends on \(x_2\). At \(x_2 = 1\) the relationship is \(E\{Y\} = 15 + 2.5x_1\); at \(x_2 = 3\) it is \(E\{Y\} = 25 + 3.5x_1\). Rather than two lines, the fitted surface becomes a twisted plane.

WarningThree rules for models containing interaction

1. Main effects change meaning. With \(x_1x_2\) in the model, \(\beta_1\) is no longer “the effect of \(x_1\)”. It is the effect of \(x_1\) when \(x_2 = 0\) — a conditional effect at one specific value. If \(x_2 = 0\) is outside the observed range, \(\beta_1\) may have no interpretable meaning at all. Centring continuous predictors before forming their product makes the main effects interpretable at average values and is standard practice.

2. Respect the hierarchy principle. If an interaction term is included, both of its component main effects should be retained, whether or not they are individually significant. Omitting a main effect while keeping the product imposes a constraint that is rarely intended.

3. Prefer one F-test to several t-tests. When several interaction terms are assessed together, a single general linear F-test (Section 5.5) is preferable to a series of individual \(t\)-tests, because each additional test inflates the overall error rate.

Epidemiologists will recognise interaction under other names. Effect modification and moderation describe the same statistical phenomenon: a third variable that alters the strength or direction of an exposure–outcome association. A moderator is distinct from a confounder or a mediator, both discussed in Section 5.4 — a confounder biases an estimate, a mediator transmits it, and a moderator changes it depending on who you are.

8.3 Interaction between two numerical covariates

The multivariable model contains six continuous covariates, and any pair might interact. Three plausible pairs were specified for testing before any were fitted, each motivated by the metabolic syndrome hypothesis that adiposity and dyslipidaemia act together rather than separately. Each was added in turn to the model of Table 6 and assessed with a general linear F-test.

NoteDisclosure of the search

Three interactions were examined and two reached conventional significance. The strongest, waist–hip ratio by fasting triglyceride, is presented in detail below. This search is reported because it affects interpretation: a \(p\)-value obtained after three tests is weaker evidence than the same value from a single pre-specified hypothesis. A Bonferroni adjustment across the three tests would require \(p < 0.017\), which this result meets comfortably at \(p\) = 0.00055. An interaction identified in this way should nonetheless be described as exploratory and reported together with the search that produced it.

The interaction coefficient is 1.1731 (95% CI 0.5078 to 1.8385), and the general linear F-test comparing this model with the additive model gives \(F\) = 11.95 on 1 and 4278 degrees of freedom, \(p\) = 0.00055.

The positive sign means the two covariates’ effects are super-additive: the association between triglyceride and fasting blood sugar becomes stronger as central adiposity increases. Because the interaction coefficient is the amount by which the triglyceride slope changes per one-unit increase in waist–hip ratio, the slope at any given WHR is obtained by substitution:

\[ \text{slope of triglyceride at WHR } w = -0.6903 + (1.1731 \times w) \]

At the lower quartile of waist–hip ratio (0.81) the triglyceride slope is 0.263 mmol/L per mmol/L; at the median (0.87) it is 0.327; and at the upper quartile (0.93) it is 0.398. Across the interquartile range of central adiposity, in other words, the strength of the triglyceride–glycaemia association increases by roughly 51%. Figure 13 displays this.

The finding is biologically coherent: central obesity and hypertriglyceridaemia are both components of the metabolic syndrome, and the model suggests their effects on fasting glucose compound rather than merely add. Two observations nonetheless temper it. The main effects in Table 14 are now negative and statistically significant, which looks alarming until one recalls rule 1 below — each is the effect of one variable when the other is zero, and neither zero triglyceride nor zero waist–hip ratio exists. And the gain in explanatory power is slight: adjusted \(R^2\) rises from 30.41% to 30.59%. The interaction is real and interpretable, but it refines the model rather than transforming it.

8.4 Interaction between a numerical and a categorical covariate

The second interaction was specified in advance rather than discovered: between age and history of diabetes. It is the more instructive of the two.

The interaction coefficient is -0.0658 (95% CI -0.0836 to -0.0481), and the general linear F-test gives \(F\) = 52.95 on 1 and 4278 degrees of freedom, \(p\) < 0.001. This is strong evidence against the additive model.

8.4.1 Recovering the two age slopes

The interaction coefficient is the difference between slopes, so each group’s slope is obtained by substitution:

\[ \text{No diabetes history:} \quad \text{slope} = 0.00836 \ \text{mmol/L per year} \] \[ \text{Diabetes history:} \quad \text{slope} = 0.00836 + (-0.06582) = -0.05745 \ \text{mmol/L per year} \]

Table 16 confirms these with their confidence intervals, computed as estimated marginal trends.

ImportantThe two groups behave in opposite directions

Among participants without a history of diabetes, fasting blood sugar rises with age by 0.0084 mmol/L per year — roughly 0.08 mmol/L per decade, a small but positive gradient consistent with the gradual decline in glucose tolerance expected with ageing.

Among participants with a history of diabetes, fasting blood sugar falls with age, by 0.0575 mmol/L per year, or about 0.57 mmol/L per decade.

The additive model of Table 6, forced to fit a single slope to both groups, returned 0.0034 mmol/L per year and no evidence of any age association at all. It arrived at that null result by averaging two real and opposing gradients.

Figure 14 shows the two fitted relationships.

The gap between the groups narrows markedly across the age range. At age 30 the adjusted mean fasting blood sugar is 4.90 mmol/L without a diabetes history and 9.93 mmol/L with one, a difference of 5.02 mmol/L. By age 70 the corresponding means are 5.24 and 7.63 mmol/L, a difference of only 2.39 mmol/L.

8.4.2 Interpreting the finding

A statistical result of this kind invites explanation, and explanation should be clearly separated from evidence. A plausible reading is that younger people with diagnosed diabetes represent a more severe phenotype — earlier onset, often poorer glycaemic control — whereas older people with a diabetes diagnosis include many with milder, later-onset disease detected through screening and managed for years with treatment. Survivor effects may contribute, since those with the worst control may not survive to older ages. This is a hypothesis consistent with the data, not a finding of this analysis. The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish among these explanations, and nothing in the model tests them.

What the analysis does establish is methodological, and it is the central lesson of this section.

TipReporting practice when interaction is present
  1. Report stratum-specific effects, not a single adjusted coefficient. Once interaction is established, “the effect of age” does not exist as a single quantity. Report 0.0084 mmol/L per year for those without a diabetes history and -0.0575 for those with one, each with its confidence interval.
  2. Do not interpret the main effects in the usual way. In Table 15 the coefficient for diabetes history, 6.998, is the group difference at age zero — an extrapolation far outside the observed range of 18 to 89 years, and not a meaningful quantity.
  3. Test interaction deliberately, and only where there is reason to. Every pair of covariates could be multiplied together; testing them all guarantees spurious findings. Pre-specify the interactions that subject-matter knowledge suggests, and disclose any search, as was done in Section 8.3.
  4. Remember that interaction is scale-dependent. Two variables that interact on the additive scale used here may not interact on a multiplicative scale, and vice versa. A statement about interaction is always a statement about a particular scale of measurement.

The contrast between Figure 12 and Figure 14 is the strongest argument in this chapter for checking assumptions rather than accepting them. The additive model was not obviously deficient: its diagnostics were no worse than any other model here, and its age coefficient was reported with a respectable standard error. It was nonetheless concealing two opposing relationships behind a single null result.

9 Conclusion

This chapter developed linear regression from a single predictor to a multivariable model with interaction, checking the model’s assumptions at each stage and applying every technique to the same outcome in the same dataset. Six learning points summarise what that exercise established. Each is drawn from a result the chapter actually produced, and each is stated as guidance for the reader’s own analyses.

TipSix learning points

1. Statistical significance and explanatory power are different things, and large samples separate them completely.

In Section 3, 15 of 18 covariates were significantly associated with fasting blood sugar, yet apart from history of diabetes none explained more than 7.6% of its variance. Marital status achieved \(p\) = 0.0010 while explaining 0.25% of the variation — about one part in 398. With several thousand observations, a \(p\)-value establishes only that an association is not zero; it says nothing about whether the association matters. Report the effect size with its confidence interval, let \(R^2\) describe explanatory power, and let neither substitute for the other.

2. The regression equation is the deliverable, and interpretation follows from it mechanically.

Writing out the fitted equation with its units makes interpretation almost automatic, for continuous and categorical predictors alike. A slope of 0.0738 mmol/L per kg/m² becomes the more communicable 0.369 mmol/L per 5 kg/m²; and for an indicator variable, the intercept is the reference group’s mean while the coefficient is the difference between groups, as Section 3.7.2 verified against the directly computed means. Rescale a coefficient whenever its natural unit is much smaller or larger than the spread of the variable — the waist–hip ratio coefficient in Section 5.3 is the clearest case. Keep the units attached, state the direction, and check that the intercept is meaningful before interpreting it — at a body mass index of zero, it is not.

3. Fit the model, then look at the residuals — and let the plots lead the tests.

Both simple models in Section 4 produced entirely respectable coefficient tables, and both had markedly skewed residuals — the body mass index model with non-constant variance as well. A coefficient table looks identical whether the assumptions hold or fail. Note too that the two models failed differently: the marital status model passed the constant-variance check that the body mass index model failed, so assumptions must be checked for the model actually fitted rather than assumed to carry over from another model of the same outcome. Residuals-versus-fitted plots reveal non-constant variance and non-linearity, normal probability plots reveal skew, and residuals plotted against omitted predictors reveal what the model has left out — as Figure 4 did, arguing for a multivariable model on evidence rather than assertion. Formal tests corroborate what the plots show; at these sample sizes they reject essentially any real data, so a significant Shapiro–Wilk result is informative only when the plot agrees.

4. Adjustment can overturn a crude result, and only subject-matter knowledge decides which result answers the question.

The clearest finding in this chapter is that age, strongly associated with fasting blood sugar when examined alone (0.0335 mmol/L per year, \(p\) = 6.9 × 10-36), showed no association whatever after adjustment (0.0034 mmol/L per year, \(p\) = 0.213). Adjustment removed a real association because the covariates transmitting it — body mass index, blood pressure, diabetes status — are plausibly consequences of ageing rather than confounders of it. Confounders and mediators are statistically indistinguishable; both change the coefficient. Always report crude and adjusted estimates side by side, and justify the covariate set on causal reasoning rather than on which variables happen to be significant.

5. Test groups of parameters with the general linear F-test, and check the assumptions that individual coefficients cannot reveal.

Ethnicity occupies three coefficients in the model, one of which is not significant. Reading them individually gives no answer to “does ethnicity matter?”; the general linear F-test does, giving \(F\) = 81.87 on 3 and 4279 degrees of freedom, \(p\) < 0.001 (Section 5.5). One test is also safer than three, and unlike the individual contrasts it does not depend on the choice of reference category. Two further problems are invisible in a coefficient table read on its own. Section 6 showed the model failing the constant-variance condition emphatically (Breusch–Pagan \(\chi^2\) = 340, \(p\) < 0.001), which leaves the coefficients unbiased but their standard errors unreliable. And Section 5.6.1 showed that adding waist circumference to a model already containing body mass index and waist–hip ratio drove all three adiposity terms to non-significance while improving the fit not at all — a model can appear to show that adiposity does not matter simply because it has been asked to measure it three times.

6. Check whether effects are additive before reporting a single adjusted coefficient.

Every model before Section 8 assumed each covariate acts identically for everyone. For age that assumption was wrong. Allowing the age slope to differ by diabetes history gave 0.0084 mmol/L per year among participants without a history and -0.0575 among those with one — gradients of opposite sign, with an interaction test of \(F\) = 52.9, \(p\) < 0.001. The additive model’s null age coefficient was the average of two real and opposing relationships. Once interaction is established, report stratum-specific effects rather than a single slope, do not interpret main effects in the usual way, and pre-specify the interactions worth testing — disclosing any search, as Section 8.3 does.

9.1 Closing remarks

Two themes run through these points. The first is that the model’s output is never self-validating. Coefficients, standard errors and \(p\)-values are produced identically whether the assumptions hold or fail, whether a crucial covariate is omitted, and whether an effect is uniform or reverses direction between subgroups. Everything of value in a regression analysis comes from what the analyst does after the model is fitted.

The second is that statistics cannot supply the subject-matter reasoning it depends on. Whether to adjust for a variable, whether an association is worth reporting, whether an interaction is plausible or an artefact of searching, and whether any of it supports a causal claim are questions that regression poses but cannot answer. The techniques in this chapter make those questions precise and quantify what the data say about them. Answering them remains the responsibility of the researcher.

Readers ready to go further will find the natural extensions close at hand. Logistic regression handles binary outcomes, Poisson and negative binomial regression handle counts, Cox regression handles time to event, and mixed-effects models handle grouped or repeated measurements. Each relaxes one assumption of the model developed here while retaining its structure, its vocabulary and its diagnostic logic. The effort invested in understanding linear regression thoroughly is repaid in all of them.

10.5 Dataset

The Metabolic Syndrome Study for Malaysia (MSSM) dataset used throughout this chapter is a community-based health survey of 4295 adults, held by the author. It is used here for teaching purposes. Body mass index and waist–hip ratio were derived from the recorded weight, height, waist circumference and hip circumference as described in Section 3.1.1; all other variables are as collected.
